# Assessing Look-Ahead Bias in Stock Return Predictions Generated by GPT Sentiment Analysis

- **Citation:** Paul Glasserman and Caden Lin (2023). Working paper (Columbia Business School;
  Columbia University). arXiv 2309.17322, v1 of 29 September 2023, the only version. Version
  read: v1, full text.
- **Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17322
- **Stream:** 08, blind replay (also bears on 03, look-ahead bias and memorisation)
- **Verified against source:** yes, 2026-11-19 (full text of v1 read as page text from the arXiv
  HTML in the in-app browser: abstract, sections 1 to 4, Tables 1 to 13 and Appendix A. Figures
  1 and 2 were read by caption only. Footnote 1 was not captured.)

## Question
A backtest of an LLM news-sentiment strategy inside the model's training window is biased. How
large is the bias, and does removing the company's identifiers from the headline measure and
remove it?

## Data
- **Period:** in-sample January 2015 to September 2021, where the paper places the end of
  GPT-3.5's training data; out-of-sample October 2021 to December 2022.
- **Scraped headlines:** 129,431 headlines on 6,723 companies, found by web search on days when
  RavenPack had news on the company. Median market capitalisation 2.59 billion dollars.
- **Thomson Reuters headlines:** 181,908 headlines on 678 S&P 500 companies. Median market
  capitalisation 56.74 billion dollars.
- Daily returns from CRSP. Delisted firms: not addressed.
- **Model:** GPT-3.5-Turbo at temperature 0. No snapshot identifier is given.

## Method
- **Scoring.** The prompt of Lopez-Lira and Tang (2023): is this headline good or bad for the
  stock price of the company in the short term? YES, NO and UNKNOWN become +1, -1 and 0.
- **Anonymisation (section 2.4).**
  1. Take the official company name and strip punctuation and endings such as Inc, LLC, Limited.
  2. Slide across the headline and compare each substring with the name by fuzzy matching (token
     set, then normalised InDel similarity). A score above 80 out of 100 is a match.
  3. Replace the match with the fixed string "Blahblahblah".
  4. Repeat with shorter substrings to catch partial names (Costco from Costco Wholesale
     Corporation), and search case-sensitively for abbreviations (IBM, GE).
  5. Query the Google Knowledge Graph for up to 20 products and services of the company and
     replace those as well (Xbox along with Microsoft).
- Named-entity recognition with spaCy was tried and dropped: it missed companies and removed
  content.
- **What is left in.** Only the target company is replaced. Other firms in the same headline,
  quarter labels, events ("Amid Pandemic"), numbers and dates stay (Table 2).
- **Coverage.** The algorithm changes 100,401 of the scraped headlines and 180,237 of the
  Thomson Reuters ones. Unchanged headlines are used as they are in both arms.
- The replaced responses in Table 4 speak of "Blahblahblah", so the name in the question was
  replaced too. The method section does not say so; this is our reading of the table.
- **Comparison.** Equal-weighted daily long-short portfolios from the original and the replaced
  scores, with no costs; paired t-tests on daily returns; a stacked regression of returns on
  each score with firm and time fixed effects and a Wald test that the two coefficients are
  equal.
- No test asks the model to identify the company from a replaced headline.

## Outcome variable and horizon
Next-period stock return: open to close, or close to close, on the trading day after the
headline.

## Result
Empirical findings.

- **Long-short mean daily return, basis points (Table 3).**

  | Sample | Original | Replaced | Paired t | p |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Scraped, in-sample (1,699 days) | 25.08 | 30.97 | -1.84 | 0.066 |
  | Thomson Reuters, in-sample (1,695 days) | 10.74 | 13.84 | -2.38 | 0.017 |
  | Scraped, out-of-sample (314 days) | 16.32 | 11.09 | 1.20 | 0.23 |
  | Thomson Reuters, out-of-sample (314 days) | 6.07 | 12.23 | -1.86 | 0.064 |

- **Regression coefficients on the score, basis points (Table 9).** Thomson Reuters in-sample:
  15.7 original against 20.9 replaced (Wald 24.2, p below 0.0001); out-of-sample 13.4 against
  22.36 (p = 0.069). Scraped: 45.9 against 49.3 in-sample (p = 0.21) and 23.5 against 23.5
  out-of-sample (p = 0.98).
- **The distraction effect.** The authors define it as every way the response to a named
  headline differs from the response to an anonymised one, apart from specific knowledge of
  what followed. Look-ahead bias can only help the original headlines. They do worse in-sample,
  so the authors conclude that distraction is negative and larger than look-ahead bias.
- **Where the losses come from (Tables 6 and 7, in-sample).** When the original call is wrong
  and the replaced call is neutral, the original strategy loses 242 basis points on average in
  the scraped set and 138 in the Thomson Reuters set. In the mirror case the replaced strategy
  loses 97 and 91. The authors call this overconfidence.
- **Error rates differ by set.** In the scraped set the replaced call is wrong more often
  (38.95% against 17.6%) and neutral less often; in the Thomson Reuters set it is wrong less
  often (under 13% against over 16%). The neutral shares are our sums from Tables 6 and 7.
- **Size (Table 8, scraped).** Companies that receive a directional call are larger than other
  companies with news: 35.4 and 42.4 billion dollars for long and short against 17.9 in-sample,
  and the gap persists out-of-sample.
- **Market beta (Table 10).** Replaced portfolios load less on the market in every sample:
  Thomson Reuters in-sample 0.317 (t = 16.6) original against 0.068 (t = 1.39) replaced.
- **In-sample against out-of-sample.** The advantage of replaced headlines is significant
  in-sample for the large-company set and loses significance out-of-sample in both sets. The
  authors read this as most of the distraction coming from knowledge of the future, with some
  remaining for large firms.

## Look-ahead and memorisation
The subject of the paper. The remedy is to hide the company and compare.

- The paper never measures whether the company is still identifiable. It notes that a headline
  such as "Blahblahblah announces release of new iPhone" gives the firm away, which is why
  products are replaced as well.
- Engelberg et al. (2025) later applied this method to Dow Jones articles and report that
  GPT-5 nano still names the firm 47.3% of the time; see our note on that paper. That is a
  different model and longer text.
- Out-of-sample is defined by the vendor's stated cutoff.

## What it settles for us
- **A raw-against-blind gap is not a leakage measure.** The gap mixes recall of outcomes, loss
  of useful context and removal of a harmful prior, and here it has the opposite sign to the one
  look-ahead bias predicts. This supports the plan's choice to measure leakage inside an episode
  (recognised against unrecognised views, and contradiction tests) and not by comparing raw and
  blind performance. Our inference.
- **Agreement with the raw call is not pure fidelity.** If a named firm distorts the call, a
  blind call that disagrees may be the better one. In S2 the information-retention metric should
  rest on accuracy against outcomes and on the increment over the statistical baseline, in the
  post-cutoff sample, with agreement as a secondary figure. Our inference.
- **A name-driven prior exists and grows with firm size.** The model gives directional calls
  more readily for large firms, in and out of sample. That is the quantity strategy G (subtract
  the call made from company and date alone) would estimate. The paper shows the prior is not
  all recall of outcomes, since it persists after the cutoff. Supported as a premise; G itself
  is not tested.
- **Name and product replacement: not addressed as a blinding method.** The paper offers no
  identification rate, and the later measurement is 47%. It adds nothing in favour of level L1
  of strategy A on text.
- **Before-and-after-cutoff comparisons need more than one short window.** The out-of-sample
  period is 314 trading days in one market regime. The plan notes the same confound for S2 (one
  clean quarter). Our inference.

## Limits
- One model, GPT-3.5, with no snapshot identifier. Nothing here speaks to current frontier
  models.
- Headlines only. Dates, numbers, other firms and event words are left in.
- No identification test, so the anonymised arm may still be partly recognised.
- The strategies ignore transaction costs and short-sale constraints; the authors say they are
  a measuring device and not feasible strategies.
- The scraped headlines were collected by web search for days on which RavenPack had news, so
  the sample is not a census of any source.
- The text gives the Thomson Reuters in-sample advantage as 81.64 - 77.27 = 4.37 basis points.
  Those are the standard deviations in Table 3; the means differ by 3.10. Verified fact about
  the text read.
- A preprint, not peer reviewed in the version read.
